title: Coexistence of myasthenia gravis and lichen planus: A case report and systematic review of related case reports from 1971 to 2024
case_prompt:
A 67-year-old man with a history of generalized pruritic violaceous papules diagnosed as lichen planus one year earlier presented with a 20-day history of mild bilateral ptosis, progressive dysphagia, and dysarthria. Dysphagia initially affected solids and progressed to liquids over 3 days; dysarthria was nasal and worsened with prolonged talking. He noted that symptoms were milder in the morning and exacerbated in the afternoon. He denied dyspnea, diplopia, headaches, vertigo, ataxia, or other systemic symptoms. His medical history included hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He had no recent infections, travel, or relevant family history.

On examination, he was afebrile, with normal blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation. Dermatologic examination revealed flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules and hyperpigmented macules on the flexural surfaces of the lower extremities. Neurologic examination showed asymmetric bilateral fatigable ptosis without ophthalmoplegia; severe reduction of the gag reflex; symmetric palate elevation; no tongue deviation or fasciculations; proximal muscle strength of 5/5 with clear fatigability, normal tone, and intact deep tendon reflexes; sensory, cerebellar, and gait examinations were normal.

Routine laboratory tests were unremarkable. Chest radiograph and noncontrast chest CT scan were normal. MRI of the brain and orbits showed no abnormalities. Motor and sensory nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography of distal and proximal muscles were normal. Repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz demonstrated a decremental response in the anconeus, trapezius, and orbicularis oculi muscles.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Ocular motor mimics were considered given ptosis but excluded by normal imaging and lack of ophthalmoplegia — “Conditions that may mimic ocular myasthenia encompass thyroid ophthalmopathy, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, myotonic dystrophy, and oculopharyngeal dystrophy, as well as brainstem and motor cranial nerve pathology.”  
2. Motor neuron disease, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, other neuropathies, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, and myopathies were considered for proximal weakness but ruled out by normal nerve conduction studies and electromyography — “Diagnostic considerations for limb weakness symptoms associated with MG encompass motor neuron disease, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, other motor neuropathies, Lambert‐Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), and myopathies.”  
3. Generalized fatigue, motor neuron disease, and LEMS were potential explanations for fluctuating weakness but did not fit the pattern of isolated ocular and bulbar fatigability — “Several conditions may mimic generalized myasthenia, including generalized fatigue, motor neuron disease, and LEMS.”  
4. Multiple sclerosis and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome were considered for neurologic dysfunction but excluded by normal brain MRI and absence of sensory or cerebellar findings — “Other differential diagnoses include cerebral venous thrombosis, multiple sclerosis, and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.”  
5. Myasthenia gravis was favored by the characteristic fatigable weakness with diurnal variation and demonstrated by a decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation — “Fatigable weakness is the clinical hallmark of this disease, defined as fluctuating muscle weakness that exacerbates with activity and alleviates with rest.”
